To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
reperfusion of a posterior wall MI results in increased T-wave amplitude in leads V2 (right mid precordial) and V3 (right mid precoridal).

Reperfusion of the left circumferential coronary artery, which perfuses the posterior wall of the left ventricle, results in larger T waves on the right precordial leads, which are opposite to the posterior wall of heart.
Reperfusion of the left circumfex artery results in greater T-wave amplitude in V2 and the increase in T-wave amplitude is greater than in those without reperfusion of this artery."
In summary, our research is concerned with
a phenomenon known as “Wellens' syndrome” of the posterior wall and the associated electrocardiogram changes.
the electrocardiogram (ECG) changes that occur after reperfusion of an acute posterior myocardial infarction (PMI) in leads V _{2} and V _{3}.
the electrocardiographic (ECG) manifestations of posterior wall myocardial infarction (MI) after coronary artery reperfusion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of a positive Wellens' pattern in the anterior leads (V1-V4) is associated with a 2-3 fold increased risk of acute coronary syndrome (ACS).
reperfusion of posterior wall myocardium is associated with an increase in TWa and an even greater change in TWa in right precordial leads, V2 and V2, compared with patients without PMI.

reperfusion of posterior wall myocardial injury, as evidenced by a new posterior wall myocardial infarction (PMI), results in a higher right precordial T wave amplitude and a greater increase in T wave amplitude in leads V2-V3 than in patients without a posterior wall infarction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ECG is a useful and inexpensive tool for identifying posterior wall infarctions and should be considered when evaluating patients with chest pain and ST elevation on ECG.
Wellens’ syndrome of the posterior (posterior reperfusion) wall can be diagnosed on ECG by the presence of large, symmetric T-waves in right precordial leads.
Wellens' syndrome can be identified by the presence of large T-waves in V2 and/or V3 after thrombolysis in patients with posterior MI.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in patients who have had a posterior infarction, the T waves in V2 and/or V3 are large.
the posterior reperfusion T-wave is not only an important sign of reperfusion but also a sign of PMI.
in patients with STEMI, if there is a large increase in the amplitude of the T-waves in the right precordial leads after reperfusion, the patient likely has a posterior wall infarction.
